trend_source: A Philippines-based creator splits a 13th month pay into buckets: 30% Christmas budget for family, 10% guilt-free treat, 20% savings for your future self and 40% bills, shifting more to savings if you have no debt. It has 1.4M views, 84.6k likes and 22.9k shares.
title: Split your AWS or year-end bonus before it hits your account
hooks: I want you to decide where every dollar of your year-end bonus goes before it lands, not after it disappears.
That viral 13th month pay split from the Philippines works for Singapore's AWS season too. Here's my take.
If your bonus usually vanishes by Chinese New Year, try giving it a job first.
talking_points: Many Singapore employees get an AWS or year-end bonus around December. Work from the amount you actually receive after CPF deductions, not the headline figure.
Set a festive and family bucket and a guilt-free treat bucket with a fixed cap. Planned spending feels better than regret spending.

Clear expensive debt first, like a revolving credit card balance, then direct the rest to your future self: emergency fund, or a CPF or SRS top-up if it suits you. Check the CPF Board and IRAS sites for current rules.
If you're debt-free, do what the original video suggests and move the debt bucket into savings. That one decision compounds.
cta: Comment SPLIT and I'll send you a simple bonus-split template you can fill in before December.
why_it_works: The original's 22.9k shares show people want a ready-made bonus formula, and Singapore's AWS season makes it timely and locally useful without any product pitch.
how_to_film: Face camera, chest-up, with a calculator or phone in hand. Say the first hook in the opening 2 seconds, then flash each bucket as a bold on-screen percentage with a quick cut per bucket. Keep it under 45 seconds and end pointing down to the comments.
author: @chelsea_dygital

trend_source: A 'poor vs rich' business story contrasts a laundromat owner who does all the work himself and loses money when a machine breaks with one who builds memberships, contracts, staff and more stores. It has 668.2k views, 64.2k likes and 5.3k shares.
title: The laundromat owner who stops working still earns. Do you?
hooks: I watched this laundromat video and realised most of us are the first owner: our income stops the day we stop working.
Same laundromat, two owners. One of them is basically every salaried employee in Singapore.
If you couldn't work for six months, what would keep paying you?
talking_points: The first owner's income depends entirely on him showing up. If he stops or a machine breaks, money stops. For most employees, our salary works the same way.
The second owner spreads his income: memberships, contracts, staff, more locations. For individuals, the version of this is savings, skills and investments built up over time.
While you build those, protect the main engine. MediShield Life helps with hospital bills, but it isn't designed to replace your salary if illness stops you working.
Do a quick check: what coverage do you have through your employer, does it end if you change jobs, and how many months could your savings cover?
cta: DM me INCOME and I'll walk you through a quick check on how protected your paycheck really is.
why_it_works: The story is already a hit because the contrast is simple. Applying it to the viewer's own income is an honest, non-alarmist bridge to income planning.
how_to_film: Open with a laundromat or washing-machine clip, or stand in front of one, and deliver the first hook straight away. Use a split-screen 'Owner 1 vs Owner 2' graphic, then cut to you face-on for the protection point. Steady, conversational pace, about 50 seconds.
author: @delta.finance1

trend_source: A 28-year-old US project manager on a debt payoff journey budgets her monthly take-home pay with the 50/30/20 rule (needs, wants, savings and debt). She admits some call it outdated but says it works for her. It has 105.1k views, 16.9k likes and 303 comments.
title: The 50/30/20 rule, translated for a Singapore paycheck
hooks: I know people call 50/30/20 outdated, but for someone just getting their money together, simple beats perfect.
Here's how a popular American budget rule actually looks on a Singapore salary after CPF.
Payday hits and everyone wants a piece. Here's a split that keeps some for you.
talking_points: Start from take-home pay. In Singapore your employee CPF contribution is already taken out, so budget from what lands in your bank account.
50% needs: rent or your share of household costs, transport, phone, utilities and insurance premiums. If needs run past half, that's useful information, not failure.
30% wants: food outings, shopping, subscriptions. Name them so they don't quietly creep up.
20% savings and debt: clear high-interest debt like credit card balances first, then build your emergency fund and long-term savings.
cta: What split are you on right now, 50/30/20 or something else? Tell me in the comments.
why_it_works: Budget-with-me content drives comments, and the original's 303 comments prove it. Localising the rule for CPF and take-home pay gives Singapore viewers something they can use immediately.
how_to_film: Film at a desk with a phone or notebook showing three labelled buckets. First line to camera within 2 seconds. Animate 50, 30 and 20 as on-screen text, using round sample numbers that are clearly labelled as an example. Keep it brisk, under 50 seconds.
author: @raquelsjourney_

trend_source: Two friends start a taco truck on a handshake with no written agreement. When one wants out, they end up selling the truck and losing most of the money to legal fees. The 'smart' version defines roles, puts assets in the company and uses a buy-sell agreement. It has 177.4k views, 10.9k likes and 1.5k shares.
title: The handshake partnership that ended in lawyers' fees
hooks: I see so many Singapore business partners start on a handshake. This taco truck story shows how that can end.
Two friends, one food truck, zero paperwork. Guess who ended up with the money? The lawyers.
If your business partner wanted out tomorrow, do you know exactly what happens?
talking_points: Write down roles and responsibilities before day one, even with a close friend. That's the first fix in the video.
Let the company own the key assets, like equipment, brand and recipes, so ownership isn't argued over later.
Agree on how someone exits. A buy-sell agreement sets that out, and a lawyer should help draft it.

Think about the harder scenario too: if a partner passes away or falls critically ill, where does the money to buy out their share come from? Some owners plan for this with insurance, so ask a licensed adviser what fits your situation.
cta: Business owners, DM me PARTNER and I'll share the questions every partnership should answer before it's too late to ask nicely.
why_it_works: The story's drama is the hook, and its own solution, the buy-sell agreement, leads naturally to business continuity planning for Singapore SME owners. The advisor stays in their lane and doesn't play lawyer.
how_to_film: Open with a napkin you scribble on and then crumple as you say the first hook. Talk to camera, medium shot, and put the three fixes on screen as numbered text. End with a calm, serious tone for the funding point. About 55 seconds.
author: @delta.finance1

trend_source: A US creator who once lived on a $36,000 salary shows how she'd split $3,000 net a month to stop living paycheck to paycheck, including 10% for an emergency fund, 8% for investing or debt and 6% for fun money. She says not to wait until month-end to save what's left over. It has 88.4k views and 6.4k likes.
title: Save first, spend the rest: a S$3,000 take-home example
hooks: I'll say it plainly: if you save whatever's left at month-end, there usually won't be anything left.
Here's how I'd split a S$3,000 take-home pay if I wanted to stop living paycheck to paycheck.
Budgets that ban all fun fail. This one keeps fun money in, on purpose.
talking_points: Budget from take-home pay after CPF. The original video uses US figures, so treat any split as a starting point for your own costs.
Pay yourself first: set an automatic transfer on payday into a separate account for your emergency fund, so you never see that money as spendable.
Keep a fixed fun-money amount. As the original creator says, overly strict budgets are hard to stick to.
Once your emergency fund covers a few months of expenses, put your savings to work toward long-term goals that suit your timeline and comfort with risk.
cta: Save this and set up your payday auto-transfer tonight. Share it with a friend who keeps saying they'll start next month.
why_it_works: 'If I made X a month' splits are a proven format. Converting it to a Singapore take-home example with a clear pay-yourself-first habit makes it practical and shareable.
how_to_film: Hold up a sheet of paper or a screen showing 'S$3,000' as the first hook lands. List the categories one by one with quick jump cuts and on-screen labels marked as an example. Finish by showing the auto-transfer setup screen with no bank branding visible. 40 to 50 seconds.
author: @jocelynbesara

trend_source: A pizza shop owner sells 200 pizzas in a day for $4,000 but keeps only $1,200 after ingredient costs and a delivery app's 30% cut. A rival on the same street skips the apps and creates family dinner bundles instead. It has 215k views and 4.7k likes.
title: 200 pizzas, $1,200 left: busy isn't the same as wealthy
hooks: I love this pizza story because it's exactly what happens when a pay rise comes in and nothing changes in your bank account.
He sold 200 pizzas in one day and still felt broke at closing. Sound familiar?
Your income isn't what you earn. It's what you keep after everything quietly takes a cut.
talking_points: The owner saw $4,000 in sales and felt rich. After costs and app fees, he kept $1,200. Revenue isn't the same as what you keep.
Our personal version is lifestyle creep, subscriptions, delivery fees and convenience charges taking small cuts we never add up.
The rival didn't just work harder. He changed the setup by understanding what customers actually wanted. Ask what your setup looks like, not just how much you hustle.
Try it this week: track one month of spending and total up every small recurring cut. Then decide which ones are worth keeping.
cta: Comment LEAK and I'll send you a quick checklist of where money most commonly slips away each month.
why_it_works: The math reveal is already compelling. Turning it into a lesson about personal cash flow is an honest parallel that respects the original story.
how_to_film: Open holding a pizza box or a stack of delivery receipts and say the first hook. Show the math as simple on-screen subtraction, $4,000 down to $1,200. Cut to you face-on for the personal lesson. Lively pace, under 50 seconds.
author: @mr.michael71

trend_source: A Singapore-licensed advisor's Mandarin reel unpacks a Malaysian public figure's wedding: a modest cash betrothal gift plus seven gifts covering retirement savings, family insurance, gold, education, health items and a shared trip. She argues the meaning matters more than the money. It reached 19.1k views, about 4.6x her usual.
title: The wedding is one day, the marriage is decades: have the money talk
hooks: I saw a wedding gift list from Malaysia that covered retirement, protection and health, and honestly it made me rethink what a dowry should mean.
A grand banquet or a long-term plan? Why not talk about both before you say yes.
Couples spend months planning one wedding day and barely an hour planning the next thirty years.
talking_points: The seven gifts in the story map to the key parts of family life: retirement, protection, assets, health, growth and a shared goal.
You don't need to copy the gifts or the amounts. The point is that the couple talked about the future before the big day.

For Singapore couples, useful topics include how you'll use CPF for a home, whether each of you has an emergency fund, how you'd protect each other if something happened, and what shared goals you're saving for.
As the original creator points out, money disagreements can strain a marriage. One honest conversation now is cheaper than years of tension later.
cta: Grand wedding or long-term plan, or both? Tell me which you'd choose in the comments.
why_it_works: The story is already resonating well beyond the creator's usual reach, and wedding planning is a natural, warm entry point to family financial planning for Singapore couples.
how_to_film: Film in Mandarin, English or both, depending on your audience. Count the seven gifts on your fingers or show them as a numbered on-screen list, then pause on the 'one day vs decades' line. Warm, relaxed tone, ending on the question with a smile. About 60 seconds.

trend_source: The Financial Diet, a US channel, argues that over-identifying with your job hurts your mental health and makes it easier to accept overwork and underpay. Every job is there to let us live our lives. It has 80.4k views and 4.3k likes, about 4.2x the creator's usual.
title: Your job funds your life. It shouldn't be your whole life.
hooks: I think a lot of burnout in Singapore comes from forgetting that our job is supposed to fund our life, not become it.
If your whole identity is your job, it gets much harder to say no to it.
Who are you outside of work? Your finances should have an answer to that too.
talking_points: The original point: when your job is your whole identity, you give it more and more time, even past what you need to, and it becomes easier to accept less.
A financial buffer gives you room to choose. An emergency fund makes it easier to rest, negotiate or walk away from a role that's draining you.
Budget for the life you're working for: hobbies, people and time off deserve a line in your plan, not just the leftovers.
Plan for life after work too. Retirement planning is really about funding the version of you that isn't defined by a job title.
cta: Who are you outside of work? Drop one thing you love that has nothing to do with your job in the comments.
why_it_works: Burnout and identity talk resonates strongly with Singapore's working professionals. Linking it to emergency funds and planning is a genuine, caring angle rather than a sales hook.
how_to_film: Film yourself doing a hobby, like cooking, cycling or crafting, for the first 2 seconds while you say the hook as a voiceover. Then cut to you face-on, calm and unhurried. Use minimal text, just one key line per point. About 45 seconds.
author: @thefinancialdiet
